## Introduction

In class, we used the Claude extension in VS Code Server
(see [the week 9 lecture](../week09/w9a_claude.qmd)).
Claude is great for chat and agent-style help,
but it does not give you **code completions**:
AI suggestions that appear in the editor as you type.
Additionally, you can only continue to use Claude after this course if your
PI supports an Ohio State Generative AI account, or if you get a personal account^[
  Note: If you get a personal account, you will be responsible for any costs
  associated with its use and it will not be OSU-approved].

This page focuses on GitHub Copilot, which in VS Code is a built-in feature.
Here is how it compares to Claude Code (as also shown in the [week 8 slides](../week08/w8a_genAI.qmd)):

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
::: {.column width="80%"}

| Feature                                          | GitHub Copilot | Claude Code |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------- | ----------- |
| Code completions                                 | ✅             | ❌          |
| Agentic chat                                     | ✅             | ✅          |
| Free use with a personal, "academic" account     | ✅ ^[Quite limited without educational benefits, but more useful as a student: see [below](#about-access-to-github-copilot).] | ❌ |
| Can be paid for with university funds            | ❌             | ✅          |
| Approved for use with institutional data         | ❌             | ✅          |
| _Often considered the best AI coding tool_       | ❌             | ✅          |

: {.striped .hover}

:::
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

On this page, you will learn how to:

- Get free extended access to GitHub Copilot as a student
- Sign in to GitHub Copilot and enable its code completions in VS Code
- Use GitHub Copilot's code completions, inline chat, and chat
  to help you with coding tasks

As pointed out in the table above: unlike the Claude setup we use in class,
GitHub Copilot is **not an OSU-approved tool**.
This is true even though the similarly named Microsoft Copilot _is_ OSU-approved:
these are separate products from the same company^[
GitHub and VS Code are both Microsoft products.
Google Gemini also has a VS Code extension with similar functionality,
but when I logged in with OSU credentials, I was informed that this is not available to us.
].
So, whenever you use GitHub Copilot, you must be aware of the data privacy implications
outlined in [the week 8 lecture](../week08/w8a_genAI.qmd).

## Enabling and authenticating GitHub Copilot

### About access to GitHub Copilot

Anyone with a GitHub account is automatically enrolled in the "**Copilot Free**" plan,
which provides quite limited access to Copilot's features, but at least you can try it out.
As students and teachers/faculty, we can get additional free access after applying for it.
While teachers can get access to the "**Copilot Pro**" plan,
which can also be bought by individuals for $10/month,
students get access to the more limited "**Copilot Student**" plan.

GitHub is increasingly vague about the limits of its plans, especially the Free and Student plans,
but here is an approximate summary (where an "AI Credit" is roughly a single chat request):

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="5%"}
:::
::: {.column width="90%"}

| Plan        | Free for whom    | How to get it                | Code completions | "AI Credits" |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------- |
| **Free**    | Everyone         | Automatically                | 2,000 per month  | ~50           |
| **Student** | Students         | Apply for education benefits | Unlimited        | 200           |
| **Pro**     | Teachers/Faculty | Apply for education benefits | Unlimited        | 1,500         |

: {.striped .hover}

:::
::: {.column width="5%"}
:::
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

## Intro to code completions

### What are code completions?

"[Code completions](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/get-code-suggestions/get-ide-code-suggestions)",
also known as "code suggestions" or, in VS Code, "inline suggestions",
are suggestions for additional or modified code (or other text)
that Copilot shows right in the editor as you type.
There are two types of code completions:

- **Ghost text suggestions** add new code at your cursor.
- **Next edit suggestions** change code that you have already written.

We'll go over these one by one.
After that, we'll turn to Copilot's chat,
and in an appendix, to **inline chat**, a related feature that also works right in the editor.

### Set up a practice file

You'll work directly in your `week09` dir while following along with this page.
Start by making a decompressed copy of the GTF file in a new `data` dir, for easy access:

```bash
# You should be in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/week09
mkdir -p data
zcat ../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf.gz > data/annot.gtf
```

Finally, create a file `copilot.sh`, and open it in the editor.
If Copilot is active, you should see some ghost text startup suggestions in the
file already:

![](/img/copilot-new-file.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a new shell script file in VS Code, with ghost text suggestions from GitHub Copilot." .lightbox}

To run the code in your file,
you can either copy it to the terminal and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>,
or use a keyboard shortcut to send the code from the editor to the terminal.
You should have set up that shortcut in week 7,
but if not, see the next box for instructions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Why a `.sh` file instead of a Markdown file? _(Click to expand)_

In other sessions, you've been typing code in a Markdown file
and sending it to the terminal from there.
Here, we'll use a file with a `.sh` extension instead,
because that makes things a bit easier with Copilot:

- In a `.sh` file, Copilot knows that everything is Bash code,
  so it will suggest code rather than prose,
  and comment lines work as prompts.
- You don't need to create code blocks with backticks.

But note that **this file is not a real shell script**
like the ones you wrote in week 7:
it is a scratch file whose lines you run one by one in the terminal,
just like the code in your Markdown files.
You won't run it with `bash` or `sbatch`,
which is why it doesn't need a shebang line or `set` settings.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Set a keyboard shortcut to send code from the editor to the terminal _(Click to expand)_

This shortcut will send selected code in the editor to the terminal.
When no text is selected, the shortcut sends the line your cursor is on
(in VS Code, your entire line is implicitly "selected" when your cursor is on it).
To run a multi-line command like a `for` loop, first select all of its lines.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

1. Click {{< fa cog >}} (bottom-left) > `Keyboard Shortcuts`.
2. Type "Run Selected Text" in the search box, and you should see the option
   "_Terminal: Run Selected Text in Active Terminal_".
3. Click on that line, then add the shortcut <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd>
   (don't worry about any warnings that other keybindings exist for this action;
   also, the keyboard shortcut is up to you, but I'd recommend this one).

:::
::: {.column}

![](/img/vscode-enter-line-shortcut.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot showing the VS Code keyboard shortcuts settings with the 'Run Selected Text in Active Terminal' option selected." .lightbox}

:::
:::
:::

## Ghost text suggestions

Ghost text suggestions are the most common type of code completions.
As you type, Copilot shows a suggestion in light gray "ghost text".
Press <kbd>Tab</kbd> to accept it, or <kbd>Esc</kbd> to dismiss it
(you can also simply keep typing, which dismisses it too).
There are two kinds of ghost text suggestions.

### Completing what you're typing

These suggestions try to complete the line you are typing,
or suggest a next line based on the previous ones.
For example, if you type `#!` in the first line of `copilot.sh`,
it's likely that Copilot will suggest the rest of the shebang line:

![](/img/copilot-shebang-oct26.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a new shell script in which '#!' was typed, followed by the ghost text suggestion '/bin/bash'." .lightbox}

::: legend2
I typed `#!`, and Copilot suggested `/bin/bash` in ghost text.<br>
It can be a little hard to see the distinction,
but the ghost text is fainter than the already typed text.
:::

When you accept the suggestion with <kbd>Tab</kbd>, the line is completed.
And it may immediately suggest a next line:

![](/img/copilot-shebang-next-suggestion.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script in which the shebang line has been completed, and Copilot suggests a next line with an echo command printing 'Hello, World!'." .lightbox}

::: legend2
Here, Copilot suggested `echo "Hello, world!"` as a next line.
:::

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> to dismiss the suggestion, whatever it is.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Not just code: an example in a Quarto document _(Click to expand)_

Copilot can help with many kinds of text, not just code.
In a Quarto document that is part of the source code of this website,
I typed the Markdown syntax to insert an image, `![](/img/claude-interrupt1.png){}`,
and Copilot then suggested the part in gray:

![](/img/copilot-useful-autocomplete.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a Markdown image link in which Copilot suggested, in ghost text, formatting options and alt text for the image." .lightbox}

It suggested the formatting options that I typically add to a figure,
and even fairly reasonable "alt text" (a description of the image),
based on the file name.

We'll talk about Quarto documents later in the course.
:::

### A comment as a prompt

These suggestions generate code that tries to implement what you described in a
comment line.
This is similar to asking a question in the chat,
but can be **faster and more convenient for small tasks**,
while less suitable for more complex questions.

Let's try this in your `copilot.sh` file. First, add the following into it:

```{.bash .file filename="copilot.sh"}
# GTF file:
GTF=data/annot.gtf
```

#### A first example

When you go to a new line and wait a second,
you may already see a ghost text suggestion that acts on the `GTF` variable.
But instead of letting GitHub Copilot go off on its own to randomly suggest
ways to interrogate the GTF file,
let's give it a "prompt" by typing a comment line first:

```{.bash .file filename="copilot.sh (excerpt)"}
# Count the number of entries in the GTF file
```

You may see a ghost text suggestion appear even with your cursor still at the
end of the line, but otherwise,
press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to go to a new line,
and wait for a second for the suggestion to appear.
Accept it with <kbd>Tab</kbd> and run the code:
does it seem to have given a correct suggestion?

"Entries" means rows in the table part of the GTF file,
i.e. excluding the header lines that start with `#`,
but this is deliberately a little vague, so Copilot may not always get it right.
For example, it may suggest a command that simply counts **all lines** instead.
In that case, you could switch the prompt comment to:

```{.bash .file filename="copilot.sh (excerpt)"}
# Count the number of entries (non-header lines) in the GTF file
```

A correct answer may well look like this ---
recall, you can use `grep -v` to exclude lines that start with `#`
("starts with" is expressed as `^` in a regular expression; not covered in class),
and then pipe the result into `wc -l` to count the lines:

![](/img/copilot-gtf-count-entries2.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script in which a comment line asks to count the number of entries in a GTF file, and Copilot suggests a command to do so." .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Shellcheck knows better, here _(Click to expand)_

Interestingly, in this specific case, we get a blue squiggly line under the command
from shellcheck:

![](/img/copilot-gtf-count-entries.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a grep command piped into 'wc -l' in a shell script, with a blue squiggly line from ShellCheck under it." .lightbox}

And hovering over the squiggly line shows a shellcheck suggestion for a more efficient
and shorter command ---
we don't need to pipe into `wc -l`, but can count directly with `grep -c`:

![](/img/copilot-gtf-count-entries-shellcheck.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a ShellCheck hover message on a grep command, saying 'Consider using grep -c instead of grep|wc -l' (SC2126)." .lightbox}

:::

You never know exactly what you'll get, but when I tried this,
Copilot suggested saving the output to a variable,
and then `echo`-ing a sentence with the result:

![](/img/copilot-gtf-count-entries-variable.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script in which a comment line asks to count the number of entries in a GTF file, and Copilot suggests a command that saves the result to a variable and then echoes it." .lightbox}

It did this consistently, with the commands below as well.
This is neat in a way, but also very verbose.
When I deleted the initial command and then added "print directly, no variable"
to the prompt comment, it stopped doing this:

![](/img/copilot-print-directly2.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script with a comment line asking to count the entries in the GTF file, 'print directly, no variable', followed by a one-line grep and wc command." .lightbox}

#### A second example

Let's try a question that is simpler but more likely to suggest code with
a construct that you haven't seen before:

```{.bash .file filename="copilot.sh (excerpt)"}
# Count the total number of lines in the GTF file
```

![](/img/copilot-count-total-lines.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script in which a comment line asks to count the number of lines in a GTF file, and Copilot suggests a command to do so." .lightbox}

What's up with the `<`?
You can ask Copilot to explain the code it suggests without opening the chat:
type your question as a comment line below the command,
such as `# How does the < work in the above command?`,
then go to a new line and wait for Copilot to suggest an answer as a comment
(if it suggests code instead, type `#` first).
Here's the "conversation" I had this way:

![](/img/copilot-explain-via-comments-crop.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of comment lines in a shell script in which questions about the '<' in a 'wc -l' command are answered by Copilot, also as comments." .lightbox}

You may not have gotten the same construct,
but you can use this trick with any command that Copilot suggests ---
including those in the next section.
This doesn't use any of your "AI Credits", since it's just another code completion (!).

#### Try it for yourself

Next, try some or all of the following prompts in the same way.
Copilot is likely to use commands or syntax you haven't seen yet;
in particular, it often uses `awk`.
Get Copilot to explain these commands,
and optionally dig deeper with Claude Code or Gemini.
You can also add notes like "_avoid awk_" and "_use only very basic commands_"
to your prompt comments, to see if Copilot can do it in a simpler way.

> \# Count the number of gene features in the GTF file

> \# Print a frequency table of all feature types in the GTF file

> \# Count the number of genes on the + versus the - strand

> \# What is the average length of a gene in this GTF file?

Finally, here are a few other example prompts you can try in the same way ---
these are more general Unix shell tasks that are currently likely just beyond
your abilities:

> \# Find all Markdown files in /fs/ess/PAS3493 and its subdirs

> \# List the top 5 largest files in the /fs/ess/PAS3493 directory and its subdirs

#### Tips and pitfalls

- Overall, mistakes are much more likely here than in the (Claude Code) chat,
  because it will use a low-tier model,
  and sometimes also because it has less context to work with. For example:

  ![](/img/copilot-error.png){fig-align="center" width="85%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script in which a comment line asks to count the number of genes on the + versus - strand, and Copilot suggests a command that is incorrect." .lightbox}

  ::: legend2
  This suggestion is wrong, because the string gene can occur in many lines<br>
  that do not represent a gene-level feature in the GTF file.
  :::

  ![](/img/copilot-error-fix.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a shell script in which a comment line asks to count the number of genes on the + versus - strand, and Copilot suggests a command that is incorrect, followed by a corrected command." .lightbox}

  ::: legend2
  You can follow up with a comment asking Copilot to fix the command, and it may do so.
  :::

- Sometimes, multiple suggestions are available for a prompt,
  and you can hover over the ghost text to see them.

- After you've accepted and run a command, go to a new line,
  type only a comment symbol (`#`), and wait:
  Copilot will often suggest a next step that builds on the previous command.
  See where that leads you, and whether it makes sense!

- Think of something you want to do,
  start typing the command yourself,
  and see if and how Copilot completes it.

## Next edit suggestions

["Next edit" suggestions](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editing/ai-powered-suggestions#_next-edit-suggestions)
suggest a change to code or other text **that you have already written**.
Several kinds of situations can trigger next edit suggestions, such as:

- Syntax, spelling, or style errors in your code, such as a missing closing bracket or quote.
- Changing one instance of a recurring pattern in your code,
  such as a variable name or a path:
  Copilot will then suggest to change the other instances as well.

(There isn't always a bright line between these two kinds of situations.)

### Fixing errors

As a very simple example of the first kind,
type the incorrect `Ls -lh` in your `copilot.sh` file, and wait a second:
Copilot should suggest changing it to `ls -lh`, with a lowercase `l`:

![](/img/copilot-nextedit-syntax.png){fig-align="center" width="35%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a Copilot next edit suggestion to change 'Ls -lh' to 'ls -lh'." .lightbox}

::: legend2
`Ls` is incorrect, and Copilot recognizes that we are looking for `ls` instead.\
As always, press <kbd>Tab</kbd> to accept the suggestion.
:::

### Recurring patterns

When you change one instance of a recurring pattern,
such as a sample ID, a variable name, or a file name,
Copilot will often suggest changing the other instances as well.
We'll go through two examples.

#### A shell script for a single sample

Create a new file `fastq_summary.sh`, and paste the following script into it.
This script summarizes the FASTQ files for sample `S63`
(you don't need to run it):

```{.bash .file filename="fastq_summary.sh"}
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Summarize the FASTQ files for sample S63
R1=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
R2=../garrigos/fastq/S63_R2.fastq.gz
outdir=results/fastq_summary/S63

mkdir -p "$outdir"

# Count the number of lines in each FASTQ file
n_R1=$(zcat "$R1" | wc -l)
n_R2=$(zcat "$R2" | wc -l)

# Write the line counts to a TSV file
echo -e "S63\tR1\t$n_R1" > "$outdir"/S63_counts.tsv
echo -e "S63\tR2\t$n_R2" >> "$outdir"/S63_counts.tsv

# Save the first read of each file
zcat "$R1" | head -n 4 > "$outdir"/S63_R1_first-read.txt
zcat "$R2" | head -n 4 > "$outdir"/S63_R2_first-read.txt

echo "Done with sample S63"
```

Let's say that you now want to summarize the FASTQ files for sample `S64` instead.
Change `S63` to `S64` in the line that starts with `R1=`, and wait a second:
Copilot is likely to suggest changing the next instance as well.
Press <kbd>Tab</kbd> to accept a suggestion, <kbd>Tab</kbd> again to move on
to the next suggestion, <kbd>Tab</kbd> again to accept that one, and so on.
Did Copilot catch all instances of `S63`,
including the ones in the comment line and in the final `echo` command?

A better solution would be to make the script work for any sample,
by having it accept the sample ID as an argument, as you learned in week 7.
To do so, first add the line `sample_id=$1` above the `R1=` line.
Then, change the `R1=` line to:

```bash
R1=../garrigos/fastq/${sample_id}_R1.fastq.gz
```

Copilot should now suggest replacing the other hard-coded sample IDs with `${sample_id}` as well.
Check its suggestions carefully:
for example, does it keep the curly braces in `${sample_id}_counts.tsv`?
Without them, the shell would look for a (nonexistent) variable `sample_id_counts`.

#### An R script

Next edit suggestions are not limited to changing identical pieces of text.
The R script below uses the built-in `iris` dataset to summarize, plot,
and test the sepal length of three iris species.
Even if you don't know R yet, you should be able to follow along.
Create a new file `iris.R`, and paste the following code into it
(again, you don't need to run it):

```{.r .file filename="iris.R"}
library(ggplot2)

# Mean sepal length per species
aggregate(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, FUN = mean)

# Boxplot of sepal length per species
p <- ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = "Sepal length (cm)", title = "Sepal length by species")
ggsave("sepal_length_boxplot.png", p)

# Test whether sepal length differs between versicolor and virginica
iris_sub <- subset(iris, Species != "setosa")
t.test(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris_sub)
```

Note that sepal length is referred to in four different ways in this script:
"sepal length" in the comments, `Sepal.Length` as the column name,
"Sepal length" in the plot labels, and `sepal_length` in the file name.
So, if you wanted to switch to a different variable,
a single find-and-replace wouldn't do the trick.

Change "sepal length" to "petal width" in the first comment line,
and see whether Copilot suggests changing `Sepal.Length` to `Petal.Width` in the next line.
Keep pressing <kbd>Tab</kbd> to see if it also updates the plot labels,
the output file name, and the other comment lines.

This works in the other direction, too:
change `geom_boxplot()` to `geom_violin()` to make a violin plot instead,
and see whether Copilot suggests updating the "Boxplot" comment
and the `_boxplot.png` part of the file name.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Code completions and your data
Code completions mainly use the file you're working in, and other open files, as context.
So if you use them only in your code and documentation files,
and don't open data files while doing so,
you are unlikely to send any of your data to GitHub,
even if your workspace contains data files.
This is different for the chat, especially in Agent mode (see below):
an agent can read any file in your workspace, and the output of the commands it runs.
:::

### Chat panel interface

As shown in the screenshot,
the chat panel has a text box at the bottom where you can type your prompts.
Across the bottom of that box are the following buttons:

- `+` adds file **context**
- `Agent` is the currently selected **mode**,
  and clicking it allows you to select others.
- `Auto` is the currently selected **model**,
  and clicking it allows you to select others
  (but this is plan-dependent: see below).
- The dials icon allows you to "_configure tools_",
  i.e. to select which tools the agent can use to answer your questions
  (not something you need to change for now).

Below the text box are buttons to set where the agent runs (`Local`)
and the permission level (`Default Approvals`): see below.

Way at the top is a `+` button to start a new chat.

### Approval levels

The approval levels are similar to Claude's
[permission modes](/week09/w9a_claude.qmd#permission-modes), but not equivalent.
The available approval levels are:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

- **Default Approvals** falls between Claude's Manual and Edit automatically modes.
  Like in Manual mode, Copilot runs common read-only commands without asking,
  and asks for permission before running other commands.
  But like in Edit automatically mode, it doesn't ask before editing files in your workspace
  (except for "sensitive" files like settings files):
  it saves its edits right away, and you can then keep or undo each one.

- **Bypass Approvals** lets Copilot do everything without asking,
  including running any command.
  But it still works like a regular chat turn: it may stop to ask you a question,
  or stop when it runs into an error.

- **Autopilot** goes one step further:
  besides doing everything without asking, it also answers its own questions,
  and retries on errors, so it keeps going until _it_ decides the task is done.

:::
::: {.column}

![](/img/copilot-permissions.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the GitHub Copilot approval level menu, with the options Default Approvals, Bypass Approvals, and Autopilot (Preview)." .lightbox}

::: legend2
The approval level menu, with "Default Approvals" selected.
:::

:::
:::

Note that neither Bypass Approvals nor Autopilot has the AI safety check
that Claude's Auto mode has:
they really skip all approvals, including for destructive commands^[
  In newer versions of VS Code, these levels may be called "Manual permissions"
  and "Allow all", Autopilot may have moved to the modes menu,
  and an experimental "Assisted permissions" level with an AI check,
  like Claude's Auto mode, may be available: see the
  [VS Code documentation {{< fa external-link >}}](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/approvals).].
(And whereas Plan is one of Claude's permission modes,
it is one of the chat modes in Copilot: see below.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### The `Local` button _(Click to expand)_

The `Local` button below the box sets *where* the agent runs.
You'll only need the default, `Local`,
which runs it right here in VS Code on your own files.
The other options hand the task off to a separate agent that works in the background:
`Copilot CLI` runs Copilot's command-line agent on the machine where VS Code runs
(here, at OSC),
`Cloud` runs Copilot on GitHub's servers (and opens a pull request with its changes),
and `Claude` uses Anthropic's Claude agent instead of Copilot's own.
:::

### File context

Just like Claude, Copilot can search and read files in your workspace
(the folder open in VS Code) by itself.
And like in Claude, you can point it to specific files:

- **The file that's active in the editor** is _suggested_ as context.
  Assuming you still have it open, you should see `copilot.sh` at the top of the
  chat box as shown in the screenshot on the right.
  However, unlike in Claude, it is _not_ added automatically:
  click the `+` button next to the file name to add it.
- **Other files** can be added with the `+` button at the bottom left of the chat box,
  or by typing `#` followed by part of a file name
  (in Claude, you used `@` for this).
- **Lines of code** that you select in the editor are added as context,
  just like in Claude.

::: callout-tip
#### File/context tips
As with Claude, it's often better to point Copilot to the relevant files explicitly,
rather than letting it search for them.
Even if not explicitly pointed to, Copilot is more likely to pay attention to
the files you have open in the editor, so when asking questions,
consider opening relevant files and closing irrelevant ones.
:::

### Modes

The second button from the left at the bottom of the chat box lets you select different
**chat modes**^[
  VS Code calls these "agents" rather than modes,
  but "mode" is clearer here, since all three are run by the same AI.].
The button will show the currently selected mode,
which is usually `Agent` by default.
Click it to see the menu with the three built-in modes:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}

![](/img/copilot-modes.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the GitHub Copilot modes menu, with the options Agent, Ask, Plan, and 'Configure Custom Agents...'." .lightbox}

::: legend2
The options in the modes/agents menu.
:::

:::
::: {.column}

1. **Ask** --- Copilot answers questions,
   but doesn't change any files or run any commands.
   Claude doesn't have a mode like this,
   which is why we recommended using a browser-based chat for general questions.
2. **Agent** --- Copilot can search your files, create and edit files,
   and run commands.
   This is the mode that is most similar to how we used Claude in class.
3. **Plan** --- Just like Claude's Plan mode,
   Copilot looks around your files without changing them,
   and writes a plan for a bigger task.
   Once you're happy with the plan, Copilot switches to Agent mode to carry it out.

:::
:::

(The last item in the dropdown, *Configure Custom Agents...*,
lets you create your own modes,
each with its own instructions and a list of tools it may use ---
for example, a "reviewer" mode that can only read your files and comment on your code.
You won't need this for now, as the three built-in modes cover most use cases.)

### Models

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}

While Claude can only use Anthropic models,
GitHub Copilot lets you choose between LLMs from different providers,
like GPT, Claude, Gemini, and others.

However, on the Free and Student plans,
you can only use whatever model Copilot automatically picks for each request ---
there's no model dropdown to choose from.
(Pro and other paid Copilot plans do let you manually pick a specific model.)

## Chat examples

### An example in "Ask" mode

Ask mode is most useful when you want Copilot to look at your files,
but not change anything or run commands.
For example, you can ask it to explain what a script does,
why a certain line in it fails,
or which of your scripts creates a certain output file.
In Agent mode, Copilot may start editing files or running commands
when all you wanted was an explanation.

To keep this first example simple,
well ask a general question that doesn't involve your files
(just note that in your actual research, such questions may be better asked to Gemini,
so you don't use up your Copilot credits).
Select "Ask" mode and type the following prompt:

> ***In a Bash script with set -euo pipefail, why could the line***
> ***zcat sample.fastq.gz | head -n 8 make my script stop with an error,***
> ***even though the FASTQ file is fine?***

Does its explanation make sense to you?

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click to see a possible answer</summary>

_Here's the answer I got from Copilot:_

-----

With `set -euo pipefail`, the pipeline’s exit status is treated as a failure
if **any** command in it fails.

In:

```bash
zcat sample.fastq.gz | head -n 8
```

what often happens is:

1. `head -n 8` reads 8 lines, then exits normally (`0`).
2. The pipe closes because `head` is done.
3. `zcat` is still writing, gets `SIGPIPE` (broken pipe), and exits non-zero (commonly `141`).
4. Because of `pipefail`, the pipeline status becomes non-zero.
5. Because of `-e`, your script exits.

So the FASTQ can be perfectly fine; it’s a **broken-pipe side effect** from
intentionally truncating output with `head`.

Typical fixes:

1. Ignore that specific pipeline failure:

   ```bash
   zcat sample.fastq.gz | head -n 8 || true
   ```

2. Temporarily disable `pipefail` around this command:

   ```bash
   set +o pipefail
   zcat sample.fastq.gz | head -n 8
   set -o pipefail
   ```

3. Use a command that can stop decompressing cleanly for small previews (depends on tools available),
but the above is the common practical fix.

Most robust pattern in strict-mode scripts is to explicitly allow this known benign case.

-----

**Be careful with Copilot’s first suggested fix, `|| true`**

`||` means "or": the command after it only runs if the command before it fails.
And `true` is a command that does nothing except succeed.
So, adding `|| true` to a line makes it "succeed" no matter what went wrong.

That solves the problem above,
but if the FASTQ file were missing or corrupt,
your script would now also carry on as if nothing happened ---
exactly what `set -e` is meant to prevent.
This is a common pattern in AI suggestions:
a fix that makes the error go away, but also hides errors you'd want to see.

</details>

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Testing Copilot's explanation _(Click to expand)_

Unlike an agent, Ask mode won't test its own claims ---
but you can easily do that yourself.
`$?` contains the exit status of the last command:
an exit status of `0` means success, and anything else means failure.

First, run the command without `pipefail`, which is the default in the shell:

```bash
zcat ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
echo $?
```

After the 8 lines of the FASTQ file, you should see:

```{.bash-out}
0
```

Then, run it again with `pipefail` turned on
(`set +o pipefail` turns the setting off again at the end):

```bash
set -o pipefail
zcat ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
echo $?
set +o pipefail
```

This time, after the FASTQ lines, you should see:

```{.bash-out}
141
```

Without `pipefail`, the exit status of a pipeline is that of its last command,
`head`, which ran successfully.
With `pipefail`, a failure of _any_ command in the pipeline
becomes the exit status of the whole pipeline.
Here, `141` means that `zcat` was killed by a "`SIGPIPE`" signal
because `head` stopped reading after 8 lines.
In a script with `set -e`, that would make the script stop at this line.
:::

When I asked it this, Copilot already suggested a few ways to avoid the problem,
but if it didn't, you could ask it a follow-up question,
like "How can I avoid this?".
You could also ask it to further explain something it said,
or to give a simpler explanation.

### An example in "Agent" mode

Select "Agent" mode. Your workspace is your `week09` dir,
which contains the scripts from the lecture and your `CLAUDE.md` file.
Let's ask for a new script:

> ***Write a shell script that prints the unique chromosome names in an***
> ***uncompressed GTF file. Use commands like cut and sort, not awk***

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Why "not awk"? And thoughts on providing constraints. _(Click to expand)_
For tasks with tabular files like GTF files,
AI tools tend to use `awk`, a powerful command that is really its own language,
and that we haven't covered in this course other than briefly this optional
[self-study section](/bonus/shell-data-tools.qmd#awk-for-tabular-data-processing).
More broadly,
telling the agent which commands to use keeps its code readable for you.
If you always want this,
you could add a line like "In shell scripts, don't use `awk`" to your `CLAUDE.md`.

Also, I asked for an uncompressed GTF file to avoid a more complicated script.
Agents can be very eager to dot all the i's and cross all the t's,
and may suggest complicated scripts that handle compressed files, check for errors, etc.
This is certainly good in a way, but there is also a cost:
you may end up with scripts that you don't understand,
and you become dependent on the AI to maintain them.
:::

- Like Claude would, Copilot will probably first search your workspace,
  and look at any existing scripts:
  you should see this being reported in the chat panel.

- It should also read the `CLAUDE.md` file
  [you created in the lecture on Claude](/week09/w9a_claude.qmd#persistent-instructions-with-claude.md),
  adjust its code accordingly, and even **write a diary entry** in the
  `doc/ai/claude-diary.md` file as instructed in that file.

- It will likely want to make the script executable and/or test-run it,
  and will ask for permission to do so, e.g.:

  ![](/img/copilot-agent-example-1.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the GitHub Copilot chat box, with a message asking for permission to run a command to make a script executable." .lightbox}

- Unlike in Claude's "Manual" permission mode,
  where Claude asks permission before it edits a file,
  Copilot **makes the edits** right away and saves them to disk
  (that's how it can test-run a new script) ---
  but they are still pending your review: you can keep or undo them,
  as we'll see below.

- When Copilot is done, you should see an "x files changed"
  (x is likely 2, as in the screenshot) message at the top of the chat box.
  You can click the arrow to see the file names,
  and click on them to open them in the editor:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-6.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's final chat message, with a '2 files changed' list (claude-diary.md and unique_chromosomes.sh) and Keep and Undo buttons." .lightbox}

- The file explorer should also highlight the new and changed files with these
  dot-in-box icons:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-7.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the VS Code file explorer, with dot-in-box icons next to the new or changed files claude-diary.md and unique_chromosomes.sh." .lightbox}

- As mentioned, you can still keep or undo the changes that Copilot made.
  When you open one of the changed files, you should see a diff view like this,
  where the lines highlighted in green are the new lines that Copilot added:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-8.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a diff view of claude-diary.md, with Copilot's new entry highlighted in green." .lightbox}

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click to see some additional screenshots</summary>

- Here, you can see that it looked at the other files in the workspace to determine
  what it should do:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-3.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's chat messages reporting that it reviewed files in the workspace before writing the script." .lightbox}

- Here, its first test-run of the script failed because it didn't use the correct
  path for the GTF file:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-4.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's chat messages showing a failed test-run of the new script with 'No such file or directory', and Copilot rerunning it with the correct path." .lightbox}

- Then, it fixed the path and asked for permission to run the command again:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-2.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a Copilot permission request to run the new script on 'copilot/annot.gtf', with Allow and Skip buttons." .lightbox}

- Finally, it talks about the diary entry that `CLAUDE.md` instructs it to write,
  and it also saves a note in its own memory file ---
  like Claude, Copilot keeps memory notes for itself:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-5.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's chat messages about adding an entry to claude-diary.md and a note to its memory file." .lightbox}

</details>

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: Check the agent's work

- Did Copilot look at other files before writing the script?
  Did it report reading `CLAUDE.md` and did it write a diary entry in
  `doc/ai/claude-diary.md`?
  Does the new script follow the shell script conventions in your `CLAUDE.md`?
- Where did it save the script, and why there?
- Did it do exactly what you asked, or did it add things you didn't ask for?
- Run the script on the `data/annot.gtf` file.
  Does the output look reasonable?
- The GTF file starts with a few header lines that begin with `#`.
  Predict what the simple command `cut -f 1 data/annot.gtf | sort -u` would print for those lines.
  Does the output of Copilot's script contain such lines?
  Look at the script to see how it handles them.

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click to see a hint for the last question</summary>

Header lines contain no tabs, and when a line has no delimiter, `cut` prints the whole line.
So each header line would show up as if it were a chromosome name.
(My script first removed these lines with `grep -v '^#'`: does yours?)

</details>
:::

Next, ask for an edit to that script:

> Make the script write its output to a file, which is passed as the second argument

When it's done and you open the modified script,
you should see a diff that highlights both additions and deletions:

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-10.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a diff view of the script, with removed lines in red and added lines in green, adding an output file argument." .lightbox}

And the final script may look something like this.
(It's using an if-statement to check whether two arguments were passed to the script,
and if not, it prints a usage message and exits with an error code.
For more about this, see the optional
[self-study section on if-statements](/bonus/shell-scripting.qmd#conditionals).)

![](/img/copilot-agent-example-11.png){fig-align="center" width="50%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the final script, which checks for two arguments and writes the unique chromosome names to the output file." .lightbox}

::: callout-note
#### Copilot custom "background" instructions

As mentioned above, and as you should have witnessed in the previous example,
Copilot in VS Code reads the same `CLAUDE.md` file as Claude.
Therefore, any persistent instructions you wrote for Claude also apply to Copilot.
It also reads `AGENTS.md`, the equivalent file that many other AI coding tools use.
:::

## Appendix: Inline chat

While technically part of Copilot's chat features,
**inline chat** is a final in-editor feature that dovetails nicely with code completions:
you select a piece of code and ask Copilot to modify or explain it,
right there in the editor.
(Claude doesn't have inline chat:
there, you would select the lines and ask about them in the side bar.)

### Modify code

When you are not happy with a ghost text suggestion,
you can delete it, modify your comment line, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> again.
But you can also explicitly request a change to the code with inline chat,
by selecting the code and pressing
<kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> (Mac) / <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> (Windows).

For example, here, I got an incorrect answer to the comment prompt
"How many genes have a description?":

![](/img/copilot-inline-1.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of an inline Copilot suggestion in ghost text that does not correctly answer the prompt." .lightbox}

So I pressed <kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> and reported the failure:

![](/img/copilot-inline-2.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Copilot inline chat box, with a message reporting that the previous suggestion was incorrect." .lightbox}

Copilot then came up with a fix, which I could accept:

![](/img/copilot-inline-3.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's inline chat proposing a fixed code suggestion." .lightbox}

Running the modified line did give the correct answer:

![](/img/copilot-inline-4.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the terminal, showing the corrected code now producing the correct output." .lightbox}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Inline chat also works in the terminal:
when you type a command in the terminal and press
<kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> / <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd>,
the inline chat box opens there and works on that command.
:::

### Explain code

To have Copilot explain code instead,
select it, open inline chat, type the "slash command" `/explain`,
and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>:

![](/img/copilot-inline-chat-explain1.png){fig-align="center" width="75%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Copilot inline chat box with the slash command '/explain' entered, above the selected line 'find . -type d | wc -l'." .lightbox}

For the selected line in the screenshot, `find . -type d | wc -l`,
you should get a response like the following:

![](/img/copilot-inline-chat-explain2.png){fig-align="center" width="75%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's inline chat explaining what the command 'find . -type d | wc -l' does." .lightbox}

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Inline chat

1. Select the command that Copilot suggested for
   "What is the average length of a gene in this GTF file?",
   and ask Copilot to explain it with `/explain`.
   Do you understand each part of the command now?
   If you also asked about this command with a comment line earlier,
   how does that explanation compare?

2. Select the command that Copilot suggested for
   "Print a frequency table of all feature types in the GTF file",
   and use inline chat to ask Copilot to change it
   so that the table is sorted from most to least common feature type
   (or, if it already was, from least to most common).
   Then run the modified command to check the result.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Inline chat counts as chat, not as a code completion
On the Student and Pro plans, code completions are unlimited,
but inline chat requests use your monthly "AI Credits",
just like requests in the chat side bar.
You can check how much you have used by clicking the Copilot icon in the status bar.
:::
